papers.title: The evolution of extreme spatial heterochiasmy in amphibians: interactions between sex-specific meiotic program and chromosome architecture
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33634v1

summary.background:
- Meiotic recombination (crossing over): the exchange of DNA segments between paired chromosomes when sex cells form; it reshuffles genes.
- Chiasma: the visible point where paired chromosomes are physically joined after crossing over; used as a proxy for crossover sites.
- Heterochiasmy: a difference in recombination between males and females.
- Interstitial vs terminal: crossovers in the middle of a chromosome arm versus near its tips.
- Telocentric vs metacentric: chromosomes whose centromere (the constriction point) sits near one end versus near the middle.
- Phylogenetic comparative analysis: statistics that account for shared ancestry among species.
- Ancestral reconstruction: inferring traits of extinct ancestors from living species; the authors say the result for deep ancestors is not conclusive.
summary.one_liner: A review plus phylogenetic comparison of male chiasma (crossover) location across 97 amphibian species, testing how karyotype features and ancestry shape the sex-specific placement of meiotic crossovers.
summary.plain: Egg and sperm cells shuffle parental DNA by swapping segments during meiosis, and the places where these swaps happen can differ between the sexes. This paper looks at amphibians, where male swaps cluster near the ends of chromosomes while female swaps are spread along them. The authors compiled male crossover locations for 97 species and compared them with evolutionary family trees and chromosome shapes.
summary.why: Most studies of sex differences in recombination only compare total map length, which can hide differences in where swaps occur. The paper proposes that chromosome shape, rather than genome size or sex-chromosome type, is the strongest correlate of where male swaps fall, and that rearrangements like fusions or fissions could shift this without changing the underlying meiotic machinery. These are model-based suggestions from correlations across species, so they are plausible rather than established.

papers.abstract: Heterochiasmy, sex differences in meiotic recombination, is usually described in terms of genetic-map length, potentially obscuring more consequential differences in crossover location. Amphibians provide striking examples of extreme spatial heterochiasmy, with male recombination concentrated near chromosome ends and female recombination broadly distributed, yet the evolution and genetic basis of this pattern remains poorly understood. Here, we combine a review with a phylogenetic comparative synthesis of male chiasma location across 97 amphibian species. Male crossover localization is phylogenetically structured, and ancestral reconstruction favors predominantly interstitial recombination at deeper anuran nodes, although not conclusively. The strongest correlate of male terminal crossover location is chromosome morphology: telocentric-rich karyotypes retain more interstitial male chiasmata, whereas metacentric chromosomes show more terminal male chiasmata. Genome size and sex-chromosome system show little association. We propose a sequential model in which sex-specific meiotic regulation first establishes a crossover-precursor placement bias, while centromere position influences which precursors mature into crossovers. This model predicts that chromosome fusion, fission or centromere repositioning can alter male chiasma location without requiring changes to the underlying meiotic program. Our synthesis highlights crossover location as a distinct dimension of heterochiasmy with consequences for genome-wide linkage, adaptation, divergence and sex-chromosome evolution.

papers.title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34798v1

summary.background:
- Spatial transcriptomics: measuring gene activity (transcript counts) at fixed locations on a tissue section.
- Spots: each measurement location; in Visium-type data a spot can contain several cells.
- Deconvolution: estimating the mix of cell types inside a mixed measurement.
- Single-cell reference: an atlas of individually profiled cells used to define expected cell-type expression.
- Pseudo-spots: simulated mixed spots built from data where the true single-cell answer is known, used for testing.
- Xenium, Visium, Visium HD: commercial spatial platforms at different resolutions.
- Ligand-receptor pairs: signaling molecules and their receptors, used to infer cell-to-cell communication.
- Regulon: a set of genes controlled by a common transcription factor.
summary.one_liner: SCATTER is a method that deconvolves mixed spatial transcriptomics spots into per-cell-type proportions and cell-type-specific expression profiles, using a single-cell reference, spatial neighborhood weighting, and Cell2location-based regularization of proportions.
summary.plain: Tissue maps made with spatial gene-activity technologies record gene activity in small spots, and each spot often mixes several cell types. This paper presents SCATTER, a computational tool that estimates how much of each cell type is in each spot and how each cell type behaves there, using a reference atlas of single cells and the spot locations. The authors report that it matched measured expression better than three other methods in most of their tests on pseudo-spots built from imaging data, and they show example analyses on breast cancer, multiple sclerosis, and colorectal cancer tissue.
summary.why: Being able to see how a cell type's gene expression changes across a tissue, rather than only how its share changes, could help link cell behavior to disease regions such as tumor edges or lesions. The benchmark results are reported only as pairwise win rates on pseudo-spots, and the biological examples are illustrative, so their broader value depends on further validation.

papers.abstract: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.

papers.title: Turbulent Epidemics: Scale-dependent Fluctuations as a Probe of Population Heterogeneity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31334v1

summary.background:
- Heterogeneity in epidemics: individuals and groups differ in how many people they infect (for example, superspreading events).
- Secondary attack rate: the fraction of close contacts of an infected person who become infected.
- Overdispersion: a measure of how much more variable case counts are than a simple random model would predict.
- Fluctuation spectrum: a breakdown of how much variation occurs at each size scale, borrowed from turbulence studies in fluid dynamics.
- Network-based simulation: modeling a population as nodes (people or groups) connected by contacts, and simulating transmission across those links.
- Self-limiting effects: mechanisms such as depletion of susceptible people that slow an outbreak without deliberate intervention.
summary.one_liner: The paper adapts turbulence-style scale-dependent fluctuation analysis to disaggregated COVID-19 case data from Germany's 2020/21 winter wave and uses a new network simulator (Epimetheus) to test which heterogeneity mechanisms, such as clustering and variable susceptibility, could reproduce the observed patterns.
summary.plain: Infections rarely spread evenly: some people and groups pass on far more virus than others. This paper borrows a tool from fluid physics, which breaks turbulent motion into fluctuations at different sizes, and applies it to case data from Germany's COVID-19 winter wave of 2020/21. The authors then run computer simulations of an idealized structured population to see which combinations of clustering and variation in susceptibility can reproduce the observed patterns.
summary.why: The approach offers a way to use the spatial and group-level structure in case data to constrain models of heterogeneous spread, which matters for prediction and for judging the effects of interventions. The text reports only a qualitative comparison between simulation and data, so the conclusions, such as the estimated 0.2 to 0.35 population limit on the outbreak, are tentative and depend on the chosen model.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous dynamics, including phenomena such as superspreading and clustering, is a hallmark of many infectious diseases. A key challenge lies in identifying observables that constrain heterogeneous dynamics. We here adapt the technique of turbulence decomposition from fluid dynamics to extract scale-dependent fluctuation spectra and correlation functions from disaggregated epidemiological data as a probe of population heterogeneity. To investigate possible explanations for the observed heterogeneities during the COVID-19 winter wave in Germany in 2020/21, we calculate synthetic observables using the new network-based simulation code \textsc{Epimetheus} for an idealized structured population. The code can flexibly incorporate clustering, heterogeneous connectivity and susceptibility, superspreading as well as temporal modulations of transmission risk and factors like waning of immunity and vaccination. A qualitative comparison of simulated and observed fluctuation spectra and correlation functions as well as the secondary attack rate and the overdispersion indicates that both clustering and variations of susceptibility across population substructures of all scales are required to produce the observed dynamics. Combined with heterogeneous connectivity, it is likely that self-limiting effects would have limited the winter outbreak to $0.2\texttt{-}0.35$ of the population without further behavioral changes after the autumn of 2020. A uniform population-wide reduction of transmission risk alone does not adequately explain the observed heterogeneities. Further analysis of the relative contributions and interplay of interventions and self-limiting effects on COVID-19 disease dynamics is required. We outline avenues towards a better integration of heterogeneity in models for predicting infectious disease dynamics and diagnosing effects of interventions.

papers.title: Normative and neural network models of multisensory integration
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32829v1

summary.background:
- Multisensory integration: merging information from several senses about the same event.
- Statistically optimal integration: weighting each cue by its reliability, so the combined estimate is as precise as possible.
- Normative model: a model built from a hypothesis about what the brain should compute, rather than from its wiring.
- Neural network model: a simulated set of connected units, loosely inspired by neurons, that learns or processes inputs; artificial networks can have billions of parameters.
- Neuron response profile: how a cell's firing rate changes with the stimulus it receives.
- Python code: a programming language; the review includes examples to run.
summary.one_liner: A review that organizes models of multisensory integration into normative (hypothesis-driven, statistically optimal) and neural network (circuit-emulating) classes, with accompanying equations and Python code.
summary.plain: This review looks at how brains combine signals from different senses, such as smell, sight and sound, into one picture. It sorts the many existing mathematical and computer models of this process into two groups: those that start from what the brain ideally should do, and those that try to mimic how real networks of neurons could do it. The authors also provide a step-by-step guide with simple equations and Python code, and compare what each approach explains.
summary.why: Combining senses is a common problem for animals and for artificial systems, so a clear comparison of the two modelling styles may help researchers in neuroscience and AI relate their work. The text does not show specific new results, so its value lies mainly in organizing and teaching existing ideas.

papers.abstract: Animals continuously detect scents, sights and sounds, which their brains combine into diverse multisensory streams. Multisensory integration accelerates learning, increases reaction speeds and helps to resolve sensory ambiguities. In studying this process, the field has developed a continuum of models; from concise mathematical equations, with a handful of variables, to artificial neural networks, with billions of parameters. In this review, we divide this spectrum into two classes: normative models start from a hypothesis about how multisensory signals should be integrated, while neural network models aim to emulate how circuits could integrate them. Together, these models demonstrate that observers can integrate cues in a statistically optimal fashion, and help to explain experimental findings, including the diversity of multisensory neuron response profiles and network architectures. In this review, we provide a didactic overview of multisensory models, complete with accessible equations and Python code, and compare their assumptions and explanatory power. We detail what has been learned from these models. Finally, we discuss how the ideas and insights from classical theoretical models can be reconciled with those from artificial neural networks, and how this convergence should shape future research.

papers.title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30955v1

summary.background:
- Single-cell RNA-seq measures gene activity in individual cells, giving a high-dimensional profile per cell.
- An "embedding" is a compressed numerical summary of each cell learned by a neural network encoder.
- A "manifold" is the lower-dimensional curved surface that real cell profiles tend to lie on.
- Density estimation means estimating how likely or common a given kind of cell state is.
- JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) is a self-supervised learning approach; SIGReg is a regularizer that pushes the latent space toward an isotropic Gaussian shape.
- The Jacobian measures how small input changes stretch the encoder's output; its log-volume here serves as a local density-like score.
- scIB is a standard benchmark for judging how well single-cell embeddings preserve biology and remove batch effects.
- Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic lung scarring disease; regulatory T cells are an immune cell type.
summary.one_liner: LeCellModel uses the log-volume of a JEPA encoder's Jacobian (JEPA-SCORE) under an isotropic Gaussian latent as a typicality score for single-cell RNA-seq density estimation, rare-state detection, and gene-level attribution.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether machine-learned summaries of single-cell gene activity should be judged by how well they capture how cells are distributed across possible states, not just by whether they separate known cell types. The authors build a model on a recent self-supervised method (LeJEPA) and use a local stretching measure of its encoder as a "how typical is this cell" score. They report better results than established methods on a standard benchmark, detection of rare stimulated cells in a controlled experiment, and two biology findings that they say arise from the embedding alone.
summary.why: It proposes treating the shape of the cell-state distribution as the main training goal, and offers per-gene explanations of the typicality score, which could help interpret rare or disease-linked cell populations. The text does not establish how broadly these results hold beyond the datasets described, so the claims should be read as preliminary.

papers.abstract: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

papers.title: Introduced cases, spread of infection in a community and travel control measures
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29584v1

summary.background:
- Reproduction number (R): the average number of new infections caused by one case; above 1 an outbreak can grow, below 1 it tends to die out.
- Compartmental model: a set of equations that sorts people into groups such as latently infected (infected but not yet infectious), detected infectious, and undetected infectious.
- Stochastic models: random-chance versions of the model, useful when only a few infections are introduced, where chance matters a lot.
- Branching process: a standard random model of how a small number of cases produce offspring cases, used to estimate the chance an outbreak dies out.
- Final epidemic size and attack rate: the total share of a population infected by the end of an outbreak.
- Exporter/Importer: the origin region sending travellers and the destination region receiving them.
summary.one_liner: A coupled Exporter–Importer epidemic model (deterministic ODEs plus stochastic Markov chain and branching-process approximations) analyses how timing and combinations of travel screening, quarantine and travel interruptions affect introduced SARS-CoV-2-type outbreaks in a destination community.
summary.plain: During COVID-19, many places used travel bans, border testing and quarantine to slow the spread of the virus between regions, but their results varied widely. This paper builds a mathematical model of two linked populations, the sending and receiving regions, to test how the timing and mix of these border measures interact with infected travellers arriving and spreading the disease locally.
summary.why: The paper's main claims are that screening only at departure cannot stop outbreaks in a receiving community whose reproduction number exceeds one, and that border triggers based on surveillance in the sending region act earlier than triggers based on local detections. These are model-based findings, and the text does not show how well they match real data, so they are best read as analytical guidance rather than established policy evidence.

papers.abstract: Travel restrictions, border screening and quarantine were widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent or delay the spatial spread of SARS-CoV-2, yet their effectiveness varied greatly across jurisdictions. To investigate how the timing and combination of border control measures interact with pathogen introductions and local transmission, we formulate a coupled Exporter--Importer epidemic model in both deterministic (ordinary differential equations) and stochastic (continuous-time Markov chain and multitype branching process approximation) frameworks. The model distinguishes latently infected, detected infectious and undetected infectious individuals, and explicitly separates recently arrived travellers in an introduction layer from the destination community. We derive analytical expressions for the control and basic reproduction numbers, final epidemic sizes and probabilities of outbreak extinction, and complement them with stochastic simulations. We show that pre-departure screening in the Exporter alone cannot prevent outbreaks in an Importer community with reproduction number larger than unity because latently infected travellers cross borders undetected. Post-arrival quarantine and screening in the introduction layer, as well as travel interruptions, can substantially reduce the attack rate in the Importer, but only when implemented with high stringency and triggered early. Triggering border interventions based on local detections in the Importer almost always acts too late because silent introductions precede local case detection, whereas triggers informed by surveillance in the Exporter provide a wider window of action. Effective protection of the Importer ultimately requires combining proactive, Exporter-informed border measures with local public health interventions that keep the community reproduction number near or below one.

papers.title: One-Step Self-Assembling Lipopolymer Coatings Enable Direct Longitudinal Biosensing in Native Biological Matrices
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27422v1

summary.background:
- Biosensor: a device that detects a specific molecule or particle, often by using a capture probe on a surface.
- Non-specific binding (fouling): unwanted sticking of proteins or other molecules to a surface, which creates false signals.
- Lipid-based self-assembly: fat-like molecules that spontaneously organize into a layer on a surface without chemical reactions.
- PEGylated lipids: fat molecules carrying a polyethylene glycol chain that repels proteins and helps surfaces resist sticking.
- Microfluidics: handling tiny volumes of fluid in channels a fraction of a millimetre wide.
- Digital in-line holography: a lens-free imaging method that records interference patterns to count and size particles.
- Extracellular vesicles: small membrane bubbles that cells release, often studied as messengers or disease markers; tetraspanins are surface proteins used to identify them.
summary.one_liner: A one-step, self-assembling lipid-polymer coating for microfluidic channels that suppresses non-specific binding in undiluted serum and enables label-free digital holographic counting of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicles from lung cancer cell models.
summary.plain: Medical sensing devices often give false signals because proteins and other molecules in blood or serum stick to their surfaces. This paper describes a simple coating, built from fat-like molecules that assemble themselves within minutes, that makes the inside of tiny fluid channels resist this sticking and still lets test molecules attach where intended. The authors used it with a microscope-based imaging setup to track tiny cell-released particles (extracellular vesicles) over time from lung cancer cells, using 50 microlitres of sample without first purifying it.
summary.why: Real-time, continuous monitoring of biological samples would be more useful than one-off end-point tests, and this coating is presented as simple and compatible with both glass and PDMS plastic devices. The text does not give comparison benchmarks or independent validation, so its practical reach beyond these experiments is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Sample-driven cross-reactivity remains a fundamental bottleneck for sensitive and selective biosensing in complex biological environments, particularly in microfluidic systems where high surface-to-volumes ratios amplify non-specific interactions. Here, we address this challenge with a one-step, biomimetic surface functionalization strategy based on engineered lipid-based nanocarriers that self-assemble within minutes into immunoassay-ready, antifouling interfaces that couple pegylated-lipid passivation with biorthogonal, site-specific probe conjugation. This approach enables rapid, tuneable, and reproducible surface functionalization, which suppresses sample-specific cross-reactivity even in undiluted serum, and supports direct, label-free digital biosensing assays directly in native biological environments. When integrated into an optofluidic platform combining digital in-line holography and microfluidics, this approach allows time-resolved quantification of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicle secretion dynamics from two-dimensional and three-dimensional lung cancer cell models using 50 {\mu}L of sample within 10 min, without isolation or purification. Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.

papers.title: Self-organized fractional silencing of pyramidal neurons under global depolarization in a spatial neuron-glial microcircuit model
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27847v1

summary.background:
- Neurons communicate through electrical spikes; "firing" means producing spikes.
- Hodgkin-Huxley model: a standard mathematical description of how neurons generate spikes from ion currents.
- Depolarization block: a state where a neuron is pushed so far from its resting voltage that it can no longer fire.
- Extracellular potassium: excess potassium outside cells raises neuronal excitability; astrocytes normally clear it.
- Excitation vs. inhibition: pyramidal neurons excite the network, interneurons calm it; their balance governs stability.
- Glutamate spillover: neurotransmitter leaking beyond synapses to affect neighboring cells.
- Neuromodulation (noradrenergic): chemical signals from norepinephrine that tune neuron activity.
- Microclusters: small, spatially separated groups of cells firing persistently.
summary.one_liner: A spatial computational model of a neuron–astrocyte–vascular unit shows how inhibitory interneurons lose firing first under high extracellular potassium, how stimulation can fragment a network into self-sustaining active microclusters, and how a damaged astrocyte region can destabilize surrounding healthy tissue once it exceeds a critical size.
summary.plain: This paper studies how brain tissue can slip into harmful patterns such as seizure-like bursts and spreading waves of depolarization, where cells become electrically stuck. Using a detailed computer simulation of a two-dimensional patch of neurons, support cells called astrocytes, and blood-vessel-linked units, the authors found that inhibitory cells switch off before excitatory pyramidal cells, and that strong stimulation breaks the network into small clusters of persistently overactive cells. They also report that a small area of faulty astrocyte potassium clearance is compensated by healthy neighbors, but a larger damaged area can tip surrounding tissue into lasting pathological activity.
summary.why: Epileptiform discharges and spreading depolarization are serious events in conditions such as seizures and stroke, and the model offers a testable account of how local astrocyte damage could spread into wider dysfunction. As a purely simulation study, its predictions depend on the chosen model parameters and would need experimental checking before any clinical relevance can be claimed.

papers.abstract: Pathological transitions in nervous tissue, including epileptiform discharges and cortical spreading depolarization, depend on the interplay between cellular and interstitial mechanisms. We develop a biophysically detailed two-dimensional model of the neurogliovascular unit (NGVU) integrating neuronal populations in the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism, astrocyte-regulated extracellular potassium dynamics, extracellular neurotransmitter spillover, and noradrenergic neuromodulation. Numerical simulations show that inhibitory interneurons enter depolarization block (DB) at significantly lower extracellular potassium concentrations and stimulation intensities than pyramidal neurons. Early loss of inhibition shifts the local excitation-inhibition balance and triggers network hyperexcitability. In the spatially extended network, exceeding a critical stimulation threshold induces a transition from heterogeneous but spatially uniform firing to network fragmentation into stable active microclusters with self-sustained high-frequency firing. Pyramidal neurons with lower excitatory synaptic input receive less recurrent excitation, which protects them from DB. By continuously releasing potassium ions and glutamate into the extracellular space, pyramidal neurons drive strong depolarization in more densely connected neighbors and push them into deep DB. Simulations of localized astrocytic dysfunction predict a spatial limit for potassium clearance defects. Small damaged cores are fully compensated by diffusion and uptake by surrounding healthy astrocyte units. However, above a critical damage size, activity-dependent potassium buildup and firing positive feedback disrupt homeostasis in surrounding units, promoting persistent depolarized centers with self-sustained, spatially segregated pathological activity.

papers.title: Topology-only Local Network Alignment, Part 2. DijSLA: Stochastic Greedy Extension for Cross-Species GO Annotation Prediction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26926v1

summary.background:
- Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network: a graph where proteins are nodes and physical or functional interactions are edges.
- Network alignment: finding a mapping between nodes of two networks so that matched nodes have similar neighborhoods; local alignment finds small matched regions rather than one whole-network mapping.
- Seed-and-extend: start from a small trusted match, then grow it outward one step at a time.
- Dijkstra-style expansion: a greedy search that always adds the best-scoring next candidate, here made stochastic.
- Gene Ontology (GO) annotations: standardized labels describing protein function; predictions are checked against later annotations.
- Precision: the fraction of predicted annotations that turn out to be correct.
- Sequence-based methods: function prediction using amino acid sequence similarity, the usual baseline.
summary.one_liner: DijSLA is a topology-only local network alignment algorithm that seeds and greedily extends matches between protein-protein interaction networks of different species, using randomized Dijkstra-style expansion and a network-alignment-frequency robustness score to predict Gene Ontology annotations.
summary.plain: Proteins inside cells work through their interaction partners, and the same kinds of interaction patterns tend to appear across species. This paper asks whether comparing only the shape of protein interaction maps, without using protein sequences, can reveal which proteins share a function. The authors build a method that grows small matched regions between two species' networks, adds randomness to sample many possible matches, and keeps the matches that recur often.
summary.why: The text reports that predictions from this topology-only local method reach precision comparable to or better than the best sequence-based methods, and that it yields more validated predictions than existing local aligners while using less CPU time and memory. Its relevance to wider protein function prediction is plausible but the text does not test beyond the April 2010 to April 2020 GO comparison described.

papers.abstract: Sequence similarity has long been a strong signal for protein function prediction, whereas the predictive value of network topology has been difficult to verify. Since a protein's function is largely defined by its interaction partners, and since similar interactions are expected across species, aligning protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks by topology alone should uncover functionally related proteins. Topology-only global network alignment has recently produced high-quality functional predictions, but it has yet to be shown that local regions of topological similarity can do the same. We introduce DijSLA (Dijkstra-inspired Stochastic Local Alignment), the first local network alignment algorithm designed from the ground up to use only topology. We adopt a seed-and-extend strategy: starting from seed pairs of proteins with similar network topology, we expand the alignment in a Dijkstra-inspired manner, following edges out of the aligned set to node pairs with near-maximal similarity. Rather than expanding deterministically, we inject randomness so that we can sample many high-quality alignments, in which node pairs with robust topological similarity "rise above" the noise and reveal functional similarity. Using networks and GO annotations from April 2010, we predict annotations validated against those from April 2020. With Network Alignment Frequency (NAF), a robustness measure that correlates with prediction precision, we make predictions with precision on par with or better than the best sequence-based methods and broadly similar to that of global topological alignment. Compared with existing local aligners, DijSLA produces larger, topologically high-quality alignments, which yield dramatically more predictions with higher validation rates, while using less CPU time and far less memory. Code is available at https://github.com/waynebhayes/BLANT/tree/master/CDijkstra.

papers.title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26949v1

summary.background:
- Serial dependence: the tendency of current perception to be biased toward recent stimuli.
- Autoencoder: a neural network that compresses an input and then tries to rebuild it; here it rebuilds clean video from noisy video.
- Recurrent memory (ConvGRU): a component that carries information from earlier video frames forward to later ones.
- Gaussian noise: random, bell-curve-distributed static added to each pixel.
- Gabor patch: a striped image patch often used to test orientation perception.
- Response autocorrelation: a measurement artifact where a participant's answer on one trial depends on their previous answer, which can distort the apparent pattern across delays.
summary.one_liner: Recurrent autoencoders trained only to denoise natural video develop serial dependence (perceptual bias toward recently seen orientations and locations) that quantitatively resembles human orientation judgments, including on an independent public dataset.
summary.plain: People's perception of what they see now is pulled toward what they saw a moment ago; researchers have debated why the brain does this. The authors trained small neural networks with a memory to clean up noisy video, with no goal about past perception, and found the networks that used memory cleaned up noise better, especially when the noise was stronger. Those same networks then showed a pull toward recent orientations and locations that matched human-like patterns in their timing.
summary.why: It offers a normative explanation: a bias that looks like a quirk may follow from the goal of handling noisy input well, which links behaviour to a computational objective. Whether this explains the human brain, rather than just matching some data, is not settled by this text alone.

papers.abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

papers.title: Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25440v1

summary.background:
- SIR model: splits a population into susceptible, infectious and removed (recovered) groups, with transmission and removal rates.
- Caputo fractional derivative: a generalization of ordinary rates of change, with an order alpha (1 means ordinary dynamics); values below 1 are often read as slow fading of past effects, or "memory".
- Identifiability: whether the data can, in principle, distinguish between different parameter settings.
- Kullback-Leibler divergence: a measure of how different two probability distributions are; near zero means hard to tell apart.
- Poisson counts and overdispersion: standard models for case counts; overdispersion means the variance is larger than the Poisson model allows.
- Plug-in forecast: a prediction that treats estimated parameters as exact, ignoring their uncertainty.
summary.one_liner: The paper asks whether the fractional order of a Caputo SIR epidemic model can be recovered from incidence data, showing it is weakly identifiable from early-phase data and that fitted orders can be confounded with transmission changes and overdispersion.
summary.plain: Researchers often read a better fit from a "fractional" epidemic model as proof that an outbreak has memory, meaning past infections affect later spread in a slow-fading way. This paper checks whether the memory setting (the order) can actually be pinned down from case counts. Using theory and simulations, it finds that early case data mostly reveal only two combinations of parameters, and that the order is recoverable only after the epidemic peak or after a large share of the population is infected.
summary.why: If a fitted memory parameter cannot be separated from other settings, claims of "memory" in outbreak data, and forecasts built on them, may be overconfident. The paper also reports that early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States fit orders from 0.6 to 1 about equally well, which bears on how such models should be interpreted; the wider impact beyond this setting is not assessed in the text.

papers.abstract: When a fractional order improves the fit of an epidemic model, it is usually taken as evidence of memory. We ask whether the order of the Caputo susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model can actually be recovered from incidence data. If the transmission rate is allowed to vary freely in time, as in hybrid forecasting models, every admissible order, removal rate and initial count reproduces the data exactly. With constant transmission and exact data the order is identifiable in principle, but the dominant term of early linearized growth depends on only two parameter combinations: the growth rate r = (beta - gamma)^(1/alpha) and the amplitude beta*I0/alpha. What is left is transient, and it is limited. We prove that parameter sets sharing these two combinations give Poisson count distributions whose Kullback-Leibler divergence stays bounded no matter how long the linear phase is observed, and that the nonlinear model inherits this bound as the population grows. In simulations, wrong orders were rejected in at most 5% of replicates when the data ended two weeks or more before the epidemic peak, and in 95-100% once the peak was included; separation began only a few days before the peak. With mild overdispersion the order was identified only once about 60% of the population had been infected, and with stronger overdispersion not even then. Fits that the early data could not tell apart predicted peaks that differed by 75%, and plug-in forecasts that ignored parameter uncertainty were badly overconfident. Data generated without any memory produced fitted orders below one when transmission changed and when the fitted model was discretized in daily steps. In early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States, orders from 0.6 to 1 gave almost the same growth rate, whatever value we assumed for the removal rate.

papers.title: Infection Spreading and Stochastic Extinction in Finite Spatially Inhomogeneous Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible and Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Systems
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26792v1

summary.background:
- Compartmental models: populations are split into susceptible, infected and recovered groups, with rules for moving between them.
- SIS model: infected individuals return to susceptible after recovery, so the disease can persist indefinitely.
- SIR model: recovery brings permanent immunity, so each outbreak eventually burns out.
- Epidemic threshold: the transmission level above which infection can sustain itself in an infinite population.
- Absorbing state: a condition from which the system cannot escape, here a disease-free population.
- Stochastic extinction: chance fluctuations in a small population can kill off an infection even when it would persist in a large one.
- Monte Carlo simulation: repeated random runs of a model used to estimate typical outcomes.
- Spatial correlation: how strongly infection status at one site predicts status at another nearby site.
summary.one_liner: Monte Carlo study of stochastic extinction and invasion-driven reactivation in two diffusively coupled, spatially inhomogeneous 2D lattices running SIS and SIR epidemic dynamics.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a disease in a small, finite population can die out by chance, and how neighbouring areas can revive it. The authors ran computer simulations of two linked regions on a grid, each following a simple infection rule, either infected people can become susceptible again (SIS) or they recover with lasting immunity (SIR). They report that an incoming wave of infection can restart a dormant region and keep it active for a long time, provided the two regions stay coupled long enough.
summary.why: The work looks at how chance and spatial contact together decide whether an epidemic persists, which matters for small or patchy populations. The text does not show how directly the findings apply to real disease data, so any practical link should be treated as a hypothesis.

papers.abstract: Demographic fluctuations can drive finite epidemic populations into an absorbing disease-free state even when the corresponding infinite system supports sustained activity. By means of Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate how spatial coupling of two distinct subsystems modifies stochastic extinction and epidemic spreading in susceptible-infectious-susceptible (SIS) and susceptible-infectious-recovered (SIR) models on inhomogeneous two-dimensional square lattices. For isolated SIS systems, extinction times exhibit approximate power-law scaling near the epidemic threshold even for small systems. Traversal times characterize the distinct propagation dynamics of SIS and SIR infection clusters. We consider diffusively coupled regions with different transmission characteristics in coupled SIS-SIS, SIR-SIS, and SIR-SIR configurations. Invading fronts can reactivate a vulnerable SIS region after its initial infection has disappeared and establish a long-lived active epidemic state. This stabilization can be induced by either a sustained SIS source or a single transient SIR epidemic wave. Spatial correlation measurements support a mechanism in which the invading activity generates an extended correlated infectious population, effectively providing favorable initial conditions for renewed epidemic spreading. Correlations develop particularly strongly parallel to the subsystem interfaces. Decoupling the regions after some elapsed period demonstrates that autonomous persistence requires sufficient coupling time beyond the first interface arrival for this correlated population to become established. Increasing system size delays invasion but enhances the probability of ultimate successful stabilization. In two coupled SIR regions, transmission can initiate a macroscopic secondary outbreak, while permanent immunity restricts both epidemics to transient activity.

papers.title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24705v1

summary.background:
- Chemotaxis: cells moving up or down a chemical gradient.
- Self-organized patterning: group structures that emerge from local rules without a central planner.
- Nash equilibrium: a state where no individual can do better by changing its own strategy alone, given what others do.
- Mean field game theory: a method for modeling very large numbers of agents by using the average population density in place of each individual.
- Timescales: how fast the cue (chemical signal) changes compared with how fast cells move; the paper finds this ratio matters.
- Population-level optimum: the best overall arrangement for the group, which may differ from what individuals settle on.
summary.one_liner: A mean field game framework models chemotactic cells that both move and modulate the chemical cues they follow, showing how decentralized populations can reach Nash equilibrium spatial patterns, with cue-modulation timescale affecting which patterns are selected and how efficient they are.
summary.plain: Some cells create the chemical trails they follow, and together this can form spatial patterns that help the group, such as clustering for shared metabolism or immune defense. This paper asks how close such cell groups, acting only on local information, can get to the best pattern for the whole population. The authors model each cell as optimizing its own position given the others, and report that the resulting dynamics produce several stable patterns, some close to the best achievable when there is moderate incentive to aggregate.
summary.why: It offers a game-theoretic way to measure how efficient self-organized biological patterns can be, and it reports that the speed of cue modulation relative to movement can change which pattern forms. The text is theoretical and numerical only, so its relevance to real cell systems is not established here.

papers.abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.

papers.title: A multilayer network-based modelling framework for epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus transmission in France
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24620v1

summary.background:
- Epizootic haemorrhagic disease (EHD) is a viral disease of ruminants such as cattle and deer, spread by biting midges.
- Culicoides are tiny biting midges that act as vectors (carriers) of the virus; their abundance and activity depend on temperature.
- Bluetongue is a closely related disease, and the model was originally built for it.
- Seroprevalence is the share of animals with antibodies, which indicates past infection.
- Bulk-tank milk testing checks milk pooled from a whole dairy herd for antibodies, a cheap surveillance method.
- A compartmental model sorts animals into groups (e.g. susceptible, infected, recovered) and simulates moves between them.
- A multilayer network represents several kinds of links between places (here: vector spread between pastures, movements within farms, and cattle trade).
- Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) estimates which parameter values are consistent with observed data, by comparing simulations to data rather than computing likelihoods directly.
summary.one_liner: A stochastic, spatially explicit multilayer network model adapted from bluetongue work is calibrated with ABC-SMC to canton-week bulk-tank milk seroprevalence to reconstruct the 2023-24 EHDV-8 epizootic in mainland French cattle.
summary.plain: In September 2023 a virus called epizootic haemorrhagic disease (EHDV serotype 8) appeared in French cattle, and little is known about how it spread. The authors adapted an existing computer model of a related disease, bluetongue, and fitted it to antibody levels measured in milk from farms across France's cantons (regional districts) to rebuild how the 2023-24 outbreak likely unfolded.
summary.why: Animal disease outbreaks often spread through insect vectors and animal movements, and this paper shows one way to combine both with routine milk testing to reconstruct spread and inform future vaccination planning. The text reports that the fit was only partial, with notable discrepancies and wide uncertainty, so it is best read as a methods demonstration rather than a settled account of the outbreak.

papers.abstract: Epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 (EHDV-8) emerged in France in September 2023 but its transmission dynamics remain poorly characterised. We adapted a stochastic, spatially explicit compartmental model developed for bluetongue to reconstruct the 2023-24 EHDV-8 epidemic in cattle in mainland France. The model represented transmission across cantons, incorporating cattle demography, pasture cover, relative Culicoides abundance and temperature-dependent vector processes. Three networks represented between-canton spread through short-range vector dispersal (pasture network), non-commercial cattle movements between pastures of the same farm (farm network), and cattle trade (trade network). Using approximate Bayesian computation with sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC), we calibrated the model to canton-week seroprevalence estimates derived from bulk-tank milk measurements. Calibration narrowed the plausible range of the baseline vector-mediated transmission parameter and favoured higher movement intensities through the farm network, although movement intensity remained uncertain. Simulation-based parameter recovery showed that calibration generally identified parameter regions capable of reproducing epidemic patterns comparable to the pseudo-observed data, although predictive performance varied among datasets and was typically lower than that obtained with the generating parameters. When applied to observed data, the calibrated model captured several features of the observed weekly median seroprevalence across sampled cantons, although discrepancies remained at some sampling times and predictive uncertainty was substantial. These results demonstrate how bulk-tank milk surveillance can inform the reconstruction of EHDV-8 epidemic patterns within a national-scale transmission framework. This framework provides a basis for future evaluation and optimisation of vaccination strategies.

papers.title: Molecular memory reduces timing noise in stochastic gene expression
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22554v1

summary.background:
- Gene expression: a gene is copied into mRNA, which is then translated into protein.
- Bursty expression: mRNA is often produced in short clusters ("bursts") rather than steadily.
- First-passage time (FPT): the waiting time until a quantity first reaches a set threshold.
- Noise: the relative spread or variability of a quantity; here, the variability of the crossing time.
- Birth-death model: a simple model where molecules are created and destroyed in single random steps, so waiting times are exponential and have no memory of the past.
- Multistep (hypoexponential) waiting times: a sum of several sequential exponential steps, which gives the process a kind of memory.
- Small-noise limit: an approximation valid when fluctuations are small relative to the mean.
summary.one_liner: Analytical small-noise first-passage-time statistics for bursty gene expression with multistep (hypoexponential) mRNA production and degradation, showing how this molecular memory changes timing noise relative to memoryless birth-death models.
summary.plain: The paper asks how reliably a cell can time an event, such as a protein reaching a level that switches something on, when the molecules involved are made and destroyed in several steps rather than one. Using mathematical calculations in the small-noise limit and computer simulations, the authors find that these multistep processes reduce timing noise, but for two different reasons. One reason is that multistep production of mRNA bursts smooths out fluctuations in how many mRNA copies exist; the other is that multistep degradation changes how the molecule level builds up over time.
summary.why: Cell-level timing precision matters for processes that depend on a threshold being crossed, so showing that "memory" in molecular steps can make timing more precise is a useful conceptual point. The text does not indicate specific biological systems or experimental tests, so its connection to real measurements is something the reader would need to check in the full paper.

papers.abstract: Fluctuations in gene expression affect the timing precision of downstream events triggered when a gene product reaches a critical threshold. The first-passage time (FPT) to this threshold characterizes the timing of such events. In conventional single-step birth--death models, reaction waiting times are exponentially distributed and hence memoryless. In this setting, FPT noise exhibits a U-shaped dependence on the threshold, attaining its minimum near one-half of the steady-state mean. However, mRNA production and degradation often involve multiple sequential steps, leading to hypoexponential distributions of mRNA production times and mRNA lifetimes. Here, we investigate how molecular memory arising from multistep mRNA production and degradation affects FPT statistics in bursty gene expression. We calculate FPT statistics in the small-noise limit. Both multistep mechanisms reduce FPT noise, but through distinct mechanisms. Multistep burst arrival reduces mRNA copy-number fluctuations, thereby suppressing timing noise. Multistep degradation instead reshapes transient accumulation dynamics, reducing relative timing noise even when steady-state mRNA noise increases. The threshold that minimizes FPT noise remains close to one-half of the steady-state mean, except for multistep burst arrival with constant burst sizes, for which it shifts to lower values. Stochastic simulations support the analytical predictions within their regimes of validity and show that these qualitative conclusions persist beyond the small-noise approximation.

papers.title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22440v1

summary.background:
- Generative model: a mathematical story of how data are produced, here how each person's ratings are generated from shared dimensions.
- Judgment space: a low-dimensional map in which each stimulus (face, artwork) sits at a position along shared axes, such as abstract versus figurative.
- Reweighting: each person gives the shared axes different importance, which can be negative, meaning they point opposite to the group.
- Nested models: simpler models are special cases of more flexible ones, so they can be compared directly.
- Held-out prediction: testing how well a model predicts people or items it was not trained on, which guards against overfitting.
- Rater sample: the group of people who made the judgments; results can depend on who they are.
summary.one_liner: The paper compares three nested generative models of how individuals' judgments deviate from a shared judgment space (same-sign reweighting, reversible linear transforms, and stimulus-specific offsets) and evaluates them by predicting unseen raters across ten public datasets of about 20,000 raters.
summary.plain:
People often disagree about whether a face, painting, photo, or joke is attractive or good. This paper asks not how big those disagreements are, but what form they take, and tests three candidate descriptions against public rating datasets. For faces, a simple reweighting of shared judgment dimensions was enough, while for artworks about 28 percent of raters leaned opposite to the group on the main abstract-versus-figurative direction, though that opposing group was much smaller when a different set of raters judged the same artworks.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Most work on individual differences in taste or judgment measures how large they are, so describing their shape is a different question that could inform how consensus and disagreement are modeled. The text does not show how far these findings generalize beyond the datasets studied, and the claim about shape depending on domain and raters rests on the paper's own comparisons.

papers.abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

papers.title: A unified cross-scale framework for the dynamic Waddington landscape
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19257v1

summary.background:
- Waddington landscape: a metaphor from developmental biology in which a cell is a ball rolling into valleys that correspond to cell types.
- Gene-regulatory circuit: a set of genes that switch each other on or off; its dynamics can be modeled as a system of equations with random noise.
- Probability density: a function giving how likely a system is to be in each state; here, how likely a cell is to be in each gene-expression state.
- Partial differential equation (PDE) with an integral term: an equation describing how a quantity changes in space and time, with an extra term summing over the population (here, cell division and replacement).
- Well-posedness and stationary solutions: whether the model has a unique, stable, well-behaved solution, and whether it settles into an unchanging pattern.
- Attractor and barrier: stable cell states and the energy needed to move between them.
summary.one_liner: A PDE-integral model couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving cell population renewal to define a time-dependent Waddington landscape, U = -log f, from the evolving epigenetic probability density, with well-posedness and stationary-solution results and simulations on canonical gene circuits.
summary.plain: The paper tries to connect two views of how cells choose their fate: the classic picture of cell states as valleys on a landscape, and the counts of cells that divide and replace one another in a tissue. The authors build a mathematical model that combines both, and define the landscape directly from how likely cells are to be in each state at each moment. Applied to standard small gene-regulatory circuits, they report that cell proliferation changes the shape of the landscape, including how stable states are and how hard they are to leave, and that under very high proliferation the landscape can oscillate over time.
summary.why: It addresses a gap between the Waddington landscape as a qualitative metaphor and quantitative models of cell populations, which may matter for understanding development and tissue maintenance. The text is a theoretical abstract, so its predictions remain to be checked against experimental data.

papers.abstract: The Waddington epigenetic landscape is a foundational concept in developmental biology, yet its quantitative formulations remain largely disconnected from the population dynamics that originally motivated the metaphor. Existing approaches typically describe either intracellular gene-regulatory dynamics or population-level cell kinetics, but rarely both within a unified framework. Here, we develop a unified PDE-integral framework that couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving population renewal, yielding a dynamic Waddington landscape $U(\vec{x}, t) = -\log f(\vec{x}, t)$ defined directly from the evolving epigenetic probability density $f(\vec{x}, t)$. Rigorous mathematical analysis of this framework establishes its well-posedness and provides conditions for the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions. Application to canonical gene regulatory circuits shows that proliferation is not merely a determinant of population size, but an active regulator of landscape topology. Population renewal reshapes attractor stability and transition barriers in a circuit-dependent manner, generating transient plasticity in some regulatory architectures while stabilizing progenitor states in others. Under highly proliferative conditions, these interactions further produce oscillatory ``breathing'' landscapes. Together, these results establish population renewal as an integral component of cell-fate regulation and extend the Waddington landscape from a static description of intracellular dynamics to a predictive multiscale framework linking gene regulation, cell-state dynamics, and tissue homeostasis.

papers.title: Indication of demographic and epidemiological data on early-stage risks and long-term epidemic burden
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19854v1

summary.background:
- Attack rate: the fraction of a group that ends up infected over the whole outbreak.
- Final size relation: a mathematical equation that predicts the eventual total infected from transmission parameters and contact patterns.
- Contact matrix: a table of how often people in one age group mix with people in each other age group, estimated from surveys.
- Continuous-time Markov chain: a random model of step-by-step changes (infections, recoveries) occurring at random times.
- Branching process: a model of early growth where each case produces a random number of new cases; it is used to estimate the chance an outbreak takes off.
- Major outbreak: an epidemic that grows to infect a large share of the population rather than fizzling out.
- HFMD: hand, foot and mouth disease, a common childhood viral illness.
summary.one_liner: Compares age-specific final attack rates with the early-stage probability of a major outbreak in age-structured populations, using empirical contact matrices from Guangzhou, Foshan and Zhuhai (China) with COVID-19 and HFMD scenarios, via a final-size relation and a multi-type branching-process approximation of a continuous-time Markov chain model.
summary.plain: When an infection enters a community, two questions matter: how many people in each age group will eventually be infected, and how likely the infection is to take off into a large outbreak in the first place. This paper uses real survey data on who has contact with whom by age in three Chinese cities to study both questions for two diseases, COVID-19 and hand, foot and mouth disease. The authors report that the age groups with the largest eventual share infected are not always the ones most likely to set off a major outbreak, so the two measures give different information.
summary.why: Public health planners often look at only one of these measures, so the finding that they can disagree suggests that age-targeted control decisions may need both. The text does not show how directly the results would translate into policy, so this should be read as a modelling insight rather than a settled recommendation.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between age-specific cumulative infection burden and the probability of triggering a major outbreak in heterogeneous populations. We develop two modeling frameworks that incorporate empirical age-stratified contact matrices: a deterministic framework for deriving the final size relation and a stochastic framework based on a Continuous-time Markov chain epidemic model, for which a multi-type branching-process approximation is used to characterize early-stage outbreak risk. The framework is illustrated using empirical social contact data from Guangzhou, Foshan, and Zhuhai, China, under two disease-motivated scenarios representing COVID-19 and hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). The illustrative analyses indicate that the relationship between cumulative infection burden and early-stage outbreak risk depends on both epidemiological characteristics and population contact patterns. In particular, age groups with the highest final attack rates do not necessarily have the highest probability of triggering a major outbreak. These findings highlight the complementary nature of the two measures and the value of considering both when assessing age-specific epidemic risks in practice.
